blocks.text: Consider the function define by \(f(x) = \tan x\) with domain is the set \(\left\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \wedge x \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\) and range is the set of all real numbers. The graph of the tangent function is shown in Figure 9.7.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "Consider the function define by \(f(x) = \tan x\) with domain is the set ... and range is the set of all real numbers". It should read: "Consider the function defined by \(f(x) = \tan x\), with domain the set \(\left\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\) and range the set of all real numbers." (Grammar only; the domain and range are correct.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why are the odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) removed? \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\), and \(\cos x = 0\) exactly at \(x = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \dots\), i.e. at \(x = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\). Division by zero is not defined, so these points are not in the domain. On the graph they appear as dashed vertical lines (asymptotes: lines the curve comes closer and closer to but never touches).
The symbol \(\wedge\) means "and".

blocks.alt: Graph of y = tan x from minus 3 pi over 2 to 3 pi over 2: three rising branches separated by dashed vertical asymptotes at x = minus 3 pi over 2, minus pi over 2, pi over 2 and 3 pi over 2. A dashed horizontal line y = 2 cuts every branch once.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.7: Graph of f(x) = tan x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Clearly the graph of the tangent function is not bijective because the line \(y = 2\) intersect the graph at multiple points. However, if we restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \tan x\) to the open interval \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), then the function with restricted domain, i.e. \(f : \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}\), becomes one-one and onto, that is invertible. This function with domain \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and range \((-\infty, \infty)\) is called the principal tangent function. The inverse tangent function is defined by \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \tan y\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "the line \(y = 2\) intersect the graph"; it should be "the line \(y = 2\) intersects the graph" (grammar only).

blocks.text_alt: y equals tangent inverse of x if and only if x equals tangent of y

blocks.text: The domain of \(\tan^{-1} x\) is \((-\infty, \infty)\) and the range of \(\tan^{-1} x\) is \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why an open interval this time (round brackets)? Because \(\tan\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is not defined, so the end points cannot be included. As \(x\) goes from just above \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) to just below \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\tan x\) rises steadily from very large negative values to very large positive values, taking every real value exactly once: one-to-one and onto \(\mathbb{R}\).
Two differences from sine and cosine follow:
1. \(\tan^{-1} x\) accepts every real number \(x\) (domain \(\mathbb{R}\)), e.g. \(\tan^{-1} 1000\) exists.
2. Its value never equals \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\): the range is open.

blocks.caption: Domain and range swap places (our summary)

blocks.text: The graph of the function \(\tan : \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}\) is shown in Figure 9.8(a), and the graph of \(\tan^{-1} : (-\infty, \infty) \to \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is shown in Figure 9.8(b).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = tan x only between minus pi over 2 and pi over 2. It rises through the origin, going down towards minus infinity near x = minus pi over 2 and up towards infinity near x = pi over 2; both lines are dashed asymptotes.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.8(a): Graph of y = tan x from −π/2 to π/2 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse tangent of x for all real x. It rises through the origin and flattens out, approaching the dashed horizontal asymptote y = pi over 2 on the right and y = minus pi over 2 on the left without touching them.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.8(b): Graph of y = tan⁻¹ x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The vertical asymptotes \(x = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) of Figure 9.8(a) become the horizontal asymptotes \(y = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) of Figure 9.8(b): the coordinates swap, so vertical lines turn into horizontal lines.
Reading Figure 9.8(b): for large positive \(x\) the value \(\tan^{-1} x\) gets close to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) (e.g. \(\tan^{-1} 1000 \approx 1.5698\), just below \(\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.5708\)) but never reaches it. For large negative \(x\) it gets close to \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\).

The graph of \(\tan^{-1} x\) is also obtain by reflecting the graph of the principal tangent function \(y = \tan x\) along the line \(y = x\) as a mirror image, shown in Figure 9.9. Observe that the graph of \(y = \tan x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).
book_errors: Observe that the graph of \(y = \tan x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "is also obtain by reflecting"; it should be "is also obtained by reflecting". It also prints "Observe that the graph of \(y = \tan x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\)". The graph of \(y = \tan x\) alone is not symmetric about \(y = x\); the correct statement is that the graphs of \(y = \tan x\) (principal) and \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) are symmetric about the line \(y = x\) (mirror images of each other).

blocks.alt: The principal tangent curve, between dashed vertical lines x = plus and minus pi over 2, and the inverse tangent curve, between dashed horizontal lines y = plus and minus pi over 2, drawn with the dashed line y = x. Each curve is the mirror image of the other in that line.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.9: y = tan x and y = tan⁻¹ x are mirror images in the line y = x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Like the sine and cosine functions, the domain of the tangent function can be restricted to any one of the infinitely many intervals \(\left(-\frac{3\pi}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)\), \(\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{2}\right)\), or generally \(\left(n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), with range \(\mathbb{R}\), to make the tangent function one-to-one. If no interval is specified, then \(\tan^{-1} x\) is a function with domain \((-\infty, \infty)\) and range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Each of these intervals is one complete branch of Figure 9.7, between two neighbouring asymptotes. Every branch takes all real values once, so any of them would work; the standard (principal) choice is the middle branch \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), i.e. \(n = 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(\frac{1}{\tan x} = \cot x\). For example (ours), \(\tan^{-1} 1 = \frac{\pi}{4}\), while \(\frac{1}{\tan 1} \approx 0.6421\) (1 radian). As before, the \(-1\) is the name of the inverse function, not a power.

blocks.caption: The three inverse functions met so far (our summary)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
How to find a principal value (the method of Example 1):
1. Put the expression equal to \(y\) and rewrite it without the inverse, e.g. \(\cos y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
2. Find the reference angle from the standard values, ignoring the sign.
3. Use the sign and the principal range to place the angle: a negative value gives a negative angle for \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\tan^{-1}\), but an obtuse angle \(\pi - (\text{reference angle})\) for \(\cos^{-1}\).
4. Check that the angle lies in the range.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps:
Given: the numbers \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) inside \(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\) and \(\tan^{-1}\).
To find: the principal value (one angle) of each.
Method: put the expression equal to \(y\) and use the definition \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \sin y\) (similarly for cos and tan). Then pick the one angle whose function value is right and which lies in the principal range: \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) for \(\sin^{-1}\), \([0, \pi]\) for \(\cos^{-1}\), \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) for \(\tan^{-1}\).

(i) Step 1: Change to a sine equation
\[\text{Let } \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = y\]
\[\Rightarrow \sin y = \frac{1}{2}\]
where \(y\) must lie in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
Why: we want the angle \(y\) whose sine is \(\frac{1}{2}\); by the definition, \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) means \(x = \sin y\).

(i) Step 2: Choose the angle in the range
\[\sin y = \frac{1}{2} = \sin\frac{\pi}{6}\]
\[\Rightarrow y = \frac{\pi}{6}\]
Thus, \(\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
Why: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\) is a standard value, and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). (\(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) also has sine \(\frac{1}{2}\) but is outside the range.)

(ii) Step 1: Change to a cosine equation
\[\text{Let } \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = y\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
where \(y\) must lie in \([0, \pi]\).
Why: we want the angle \(y\) whose cosine is \(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

(ii) Step 2: Choose the angle in the range
The reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), since \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). The cosine is negative, so in \([0, \pi]\) the angle is in the second quadrant:
\[y = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\]
\[\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
Thus, \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \frac{5\pi}{6}\).
Why: \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\), and \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) lies in \([0, \pi]\). A negative angle such as \(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\) is not allowed for \(\cos^{-1}\).

(iii) Step 1: Change to a tangent equation
\[\text{Let } \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = y\]
\[\Rightarrow \tan y = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\]
where \(y\) must lie in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
Why: by definition \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \tan y\).

(iii) Step 2: Choose the angle in the range
\[\tan y = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\]
\[\Rightarrow y = -\frac{\pi}{6}\]
Hence, \(\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{6}\).
Why: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and tangent is odd, \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\). The tangent is negative, so in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) the angle is negative (fourth quadrant). \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) also has tangent \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) but is outside the range.

Check:
\[\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2},\ \ \frac{\pi}{6} \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
\[\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\ \ \frac{5\pi}{6} \in [0, \pi]\]
\[\tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\]
and \(-\frac{\pi}{6} \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Each answer has the right function value and lies in the right principal range.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Principal tangent function: \(\tan : \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}\), which is bijective.
2. \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \tan y\), with domain \(\mathbb{R}\) and range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) (open).
3. The graph of \(\tan^{-1} x\) has horizontal asymptotes \(y = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\); it is the mirror image of the principal tangent graph in \(y = x\).
4. Principal ranges: \(\sin^{-1}\): \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); \(\cos^{-1}\): \([0, \pi]\); \(\tan^{-1}\): \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
5. \(\tan^{-1} x\) is not \(\frac{1}{\tan x}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{5\pi}{6}\): it is outside \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\); the answer is \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\).
2. Writing \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{6}\) or \(-\frac{5\pi}{6}\): \(\cos^{-1}\) is never negative; the answer is \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\).
3. Including the end points: \(\tan^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) has no solution, because \(\tan\frac{\pi}{2}\) is undefined.
4. Thinking \(\tan^{-1} x\) needs \(-1 \le x \le 1\) like \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\cos^{-1}\): its domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
